# Synthesis: assess · T16

## Claude Opus 5.5


# TRL assessment: T16 Anchoring, hold-down and surface mobility on low-cohesion bodies

**Re-rating of `asteroid-mining-bucket-wheel`.** This assessment splits off the anchoring and hold-down element and re-scopes it.

## Summary

- **Current TRL:** 2–3. The rubble-pile variant is at 2. The monolith variant is at 2–3.
- **Target:** TRL 6 at KDP-0B.
- **AD²:** 7.
- **Risk if it fails:** project-ending for 0B as currently architected.
- **Main finding:** TRL 5–6 for this technology cannot be closed on the ground. The in-situ demonstration on a target-class NEA is the critical path, and the scouts and pathfinder must carry it.
- **Change from the March 2026 entry:** its TRL 3 rested on "multi-model consensus" and terrestrial analogues. Neither is evidence under the rating rules, so that rating is withdrawn. Its fallback, thermal volatile extraction, no longer applies: the product is now native Fe-Ni, and thermal extraction still needs contact, handling and hold-down.

## 0. Requirement as I interpret it (assumptions stated)

| Element | Required scale | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Robot anchoring (excavation reaction) | 6–20 robots, 2–3.5 t each | Revised architecture |
| Net cutting force | Peak about 0.5–20 kN | **Assumption.** P/v_tip at 10–20 kW and 1–2 m/s tip speed. In loose rubble the steady force is probably 10–100× lower. Clast strikes and monolith cuts set the peak. |
| Torque | Residual 0.25–5 kN·m with counter-rotation; 2.5–95 kN·m single-wheel | rq-0-26 re-assessment (Claude figures) |
| Duty | 9–25% over ≥5 yr, i.e. about 4,000–11,000 h excavating per robot | — |
| Load cycles | About 10⁶–10⁷ | At bucket-passage frequency |
| Anchor set/release cycles | About 10³ per robot | Re-anchoring as the face advances |
| Mobility | Translation between faces of 2–3.5 t vehicles on a 1–3 kV tether | — |
| Plant hold-down | 2.5–8 MW site. Arrays about 1.5–4 × 10⁴ m² at 20–30% cell efficiency. Plant mass unspecified (**assume 50–500 t**). | — |
| Plant loads | Solar radiation pressure about 0.1–0.3 N; thermal loads; tether loads | — |
| Gemini route only | Reaction of a 0.05–0.15 g rotating furnace (spin-up/down momentum) | — |
| Tailings hold-down | 13–47 kt/yr, about 65–235 kt cumulative over 5 yr | — |
| Tailings retention | Loss ≤1 t/yr means retention **≥99.992–99.998%** | D-03 interim ceiling |
| Environment, gravity | 10⁻⁵–3 × 10⁻⁴ m/s²; v_esc about 0.05–0.5 m/s | — |
| Environment, rubble-pile surface | Cohesion of order 0.1–100 Pa | — |
| Environment, rock | Boulder tensile strength of order 0.1–2 MPa. Competent chondrite or Fe-Ni: MPa to hundreds of MPa. | — |
| Environment, thermal | Surface about 150–400 K; about 3,600–22,000 thermal cycles/yr | — |
| Environment, other | Electrostatic dust | — |
| Environment, fast-rotator monoliths | Net centrifugal-dominated surface: loose items leave | — |

### Physics point that drives the rating

Frictional anchors (flukes, screws, piles) get their capacity from overburden stress, ρgz.

- Near the surface of a 500 m rubble pile, ρgz ≈ 1,300 × 10⁻⁴ × 1 m ≈ 0.1 Pa.
- Even the central pressure is only of order 10 Pa: (2π/3)Gρ²R² ≈ 13 Pa at ρ = 1,200 kg/m³ and R = 250 m.

Holding kN loads in such a body therefore cannot rely on friction. It must come from one of three sources:

- **Rock contact:** gripping boulders or bedrock.
- **Artificial cohesion:** grouting, sintering, or bagging.
- **Geometry:** a body-encircling girdle or net.

None of these has been tested against a prediction in a medium that is scaled to Pa-level cohesion.

## 1. Evidence

### Small-body surface-contact heritage

All entries are physical or flight data. None is anchoring under sustained load.

| MUPUS penetrator could not penetrate a hard near-surface layer | Spohn et al., *Science* 2015 | Single hammering probe, about 1 cm scale | n/a (shows failure mode) | Yes |
| Self-hammering penetrator (HP³ "mole") failed for lack of soil friction and reaction. Directly relevant to low-overburden penetration. | NASA/DLR InSight, 2019–2021 | Mars, 0.38 g | Gravity about 10³–10⁴× higher than an NEA. Failure-mode evidence only. | Yes |
| Sampler sank about 0.5 m into Bennu with very low resistance. Near-subsurface has near-zero cohesion and loose packing. | OSIRIS-REx TAG, 2020. Lauretta et al., *Science* 2022; Walsh et al., *Science Advances* 2022 | About 6 s contact, about 10 cm/s, about 2 t spacecraft | Duration ≈ 3 × 10⁷× | Qualitative: yes. Exact resistance values: unsure. |
| Gravity-dominated cratering in very-low-cohesion regolith on Ryugu (crater of order 15 m) | Hayabusa2 SCI, 2019. Arakawa et al., *Science* 2020 | 2 kg impactor at about 2 km/s | n/a (property evidence) | Yes. Exact cohesion bound: unsure. |
| Ryugu boulders are weak: tensile strength of order 0.2–0.3 MPa | MASCOT/MARA. Grott et al., *Nature Astronomy* 2019 | Thermal inference, not mechanical test | n/a | Mostly. Exact values: unsure. |
| Bennu boulder strengths of order 0.1–1 MPa | Rozitis et al., *Science Advances* 2020 | Thermal inference | n/a | Unsure of exact figures |

### Laboratory and analysis heritage

| Claim | Source | Demonstrated scale | Ratio to requirement | Confident |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Microspine grippers anchor to rough rock independent of gravity, with load-sharing models | Parness et al., *Journal of Field Robotics* 2013 (JPL) | Lab, about 10² N per gripper (**exact figure unsure**) | Force 10–200× | Paper: yes. Load values and any zero-g aircraft tests: unsure. |
| Cohesion/weight scaling: cm-grains at µg behave like µm-grains at 1 g, enabling cohesion-scaled ground analogues | Scheeres, Hartzell, Sánchez & Swift, *Icarus* 2010 | Analysis | n/a (method) | Yes |

ISAE drop-tower work, about 2017–2021 | Seconds-long, cm–dm probes | Duration about 10⁷–10⁸×; force 10³× | Programmes exist: yes. Specifics: unsure. |
| Long-duration regolith-simulant behaviour in µg | STRATA-1 on ISS, about 2016–2017 (NASA JSC) | Sealed tubes, no anchor loads | n/a | Existence: yes. Results: unsure. |

### Evidence not counted

- The rq-0-26 deliberation conclusion and any multi-model consensus.
- ARM robotic-boulder-capture design work. Ground tests may exist, but I cannot cite them confidently.

## 2. Current TRL: 2–3

| Variant | TRL | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Rubble-pile anchoring at kN load | 2 | Concepts documented (grouted/sintered anchors, girdles, boulder grip). No experiment validates holding-capacity predictions in cohesion-scaled media. |
| Monolith anchoring | 2–3 | Microspine and bolt critical function proven on rock in the lab. Not shown at kN class. Drill/bolt bootstrap in µg not shown. |
| Tethered surface mobility (2–3.5 t) | 2 | Concept only. Hopping heritage is not applicable. |
| Plant hold-down | 2 | Concepts only. |
| Tailings hold-down at ≥99.99% retention | 2 | Bagging, compaction and sintering are concepts only. Retention never measured. |

- **Met at the lower bound (TRL 2):** documented application concepts addressing feasibility. TRL 1 is clearly met by the published small-body regolith science.
- **Unmet for TRL 3 (rubble-pile, mobility, tailings):** "Documented analytical or experimental results validating predictions of key parameters." No pull-out, cyclic-load or retention test has been run in Pa-cohesion or cohesion-scaled media against a prior prediction.
- **Unmet for TRL 4 (monolith, the upper bound):** two things are missing.
  - A documented definition of the relevant environment: target boulder or bedrock strength is only thermally inferred.
  - A breadboard test at the load class (kN, 10⁶+ cycles) agreeing with prediction.

**Composite rating.** The requirement covers both variants, and the target is not yet selected under the D-02 target gate. The composite is therefore governed by the weaker variant: min 2, max 3.

## 3. Target and difficulty

### Target TRL

- **KDP-0B:** TRL 6 in a relevant environment, with no waivers.
  - Without hold-down there is no surface excavation.
  - Without tailings retention there is no licence under the D-02 licence gate (D-03 ceiling).
- **Internal 0A milestones:**
  - TRL 4 by the 0A mid-term review.
  - TRL 5 before the pathfinder design freeze.

### When it is needed

KDP-0B. Its date is not stated in the brief. **I assume no earlier than about 2034–2037**, given scout cruise times.

The 5-yr duration cannot physically be demonstrated in situ before KDP-0B. TRL 6 therefore has to rest on three things:

- At least 6–12 months of in-situ anchored operation.
- Accelerated cyclic and thermal ground testing.
- Validated degradation models.

If the board reads "no waivers" as requiring 5 yr in situ, KDP-0B slips by about 5 yr. That must be decided now, not at KDP-0B.

### AD² = 7

"Requires new approaches; fundamental engineering research," about 50% success.

**Rubble-pile variant (drives the 7):**

- Conventional anchor physics fails at about 0.1–10 Pa overburden.
- The candidate approaches (artificial cohesion, girdles, boulder grip) are untested.
- Multi-year ratcheting and creep of anchors in µg granular media under 10⁴–10⁵ thermal cycles is unknown.
- No ground facility reproduces the environment for longer than seconds.

AD² 8 is defensible here: subsurface strength and cohesion distributions are a scientific unknown that only scouts can resolve.

**Monolith variant:** 5 on its own. The path is clear: microspine bootstrap, then drilled bolts. It has simply not been done.

**Mobility and tailings:** 6–7.

## 4. Path

Costs and durations below are my estimates, not quotes.

| # | Step | Method | Scale | Cost (US$) | Duration | Reaches |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Environment and load envelope: synthesise Bennu, Ryugu, Itokawa, Eros and Dimorphos strength and cohesion data. Couple to the rq-0-26 DEM force/torque spectra. Write the relevant-environment definition per variant. | Literature + analysis | Desk | 0.5–2 M | 0.5–1 yr | 2 (prerequisite for 4) |
| 2 | Anchor critical-function tests: pull-out and cyclic tests vs prediction for microspines and drilled expansion bolts in boulder simulants (0.1–2 MPa) and Fe-Ni; grouted/sintered anchors in cohesion-scaled granular media (Scheeres 2010 scaling); subscale girdle/net | Experiment | 1–20 kN, 10⁶ cycles, vacuum thermal cycling 150–400 K | 5–15 M | 2–3 yr | 3 (rubble) / 4 (monolith) |
| 3 | Tailings retention breadboard: bagging, compaction and sinter-blocking of no-melt fines and smelter slag. Measure the loss fraction against ≥99.99%. | Experiment | 10–100 kg batches | 2–6 M | 1–2 yr | 3–4 |
| 4 | Tethered anchor-walk/crawl mobility breadboard | Experiment | Gravity-offloaded, 1/3-scale robot | 3–10 M | 1.5–3 yr | 4 |
| 5 | Reduced-gravity component tests: drop tower/Atwood, parabolic, suborbital. Plus an ISS or free-flyer long-duration granular-anchor creep experiment (STRATA-type, loaded). | Experiment | cm–dm anchors; seconds to months | 10–40 M | 2–4 yr | 4–5 |
| 6 | In-situ geotechnical payload on 0A scouts: penetrometer, shear vane, pull-out, boulder grip trial | Experiment (flight) | 10–30 kg instrument per scout | 20–60 M per instrumented scout | 4–7 yr incl. cruise | 5 |
| 7 | Pathfinder hold-down demonstration on a target-class NEA (details below) | Experiment (flight) | 200–500 kg anchored module | 150–500 M (share of pathfinder) | 3–6 yr | 6 |

**Step 7 content:**

- An anchored module reacting at least 10–30% of design load. It must include the residual torque set by the excavation design selected under rq-0-26 (0.25–5 kN·m counter-rotated; 2.5–95 kN·m single-wheel).
- At least 6–12 months of operation.
- Plant-mount and tailings-containment sub-demonstrations.
- Supplemented by the accelerated 5-yr-equivalent ground life test from step 2.

**Effect of target class on the path.** If the D-02 target gate picks a single body class early, steps 2 and 7 need only that variant. This roughly halves the cost and the time.

**Interface with the metallurgy routes:**

| Route | Effect on hold-down |
|---|---|
| No-melt (Claude) | Leaves fines, the worst case for retention. Needs an added compaction or sintering step. |
| Rotating smelter (Gemini) | Yields castable slag. That eases tailings retention and could provide ballast blocks, but adds spin-reaction loads to the plant mount. |
| Native-metal / gated hypothesis (GPT) | Sits between the two. |

## 5. Risk and fallback

### Risk class: project-ending for 0B as currently architected

Failure means two things:

- No licensable surface operation (licence gate).
- No reaction for excavation.

### Fallback

1. **Enclosed capture-and-ingest.** Bag small boulders or a whole small (<10–20 m) body and process inside an enclosure. No surface hold-down is needed. This changes the target class and throughput, and is itself only TRL 2.
2. **Otherwise,** the D-02 pre-committed "0A only, Earth supply."

Choosing a monolith target reduces difficulty to AD² 5 for anchoring. It does not remove the tailings problem.

## 6. Where others might disagree

1. **TRL 3 now.** Some will credit TRL 3 from OSIRIS-REx TAG, Hayabusa2 SCI and low-g penetration experiments. I do not: those data validate regolith properties, not anchor function at the required loads.
2. **Risk class.** "Architecture-change" is defensible if enclosed capture is accepted as a credible alternative. I rate it project-ending because that alternative is no more mature.
3. **No frictional anchoring in rubble piles.** My argument is an order-of-magnitude one. Boulder interlock or compacted interiors could give more capacity than ρgz suggests. Only in-situ pull-out data will settle it.
4. **TRL 6 without 5 yr in situ.** This is a governance call, not a technical one. It must be decided at 0A start.
5. **Counter-rotation.** Gemini treats it as solving the reaction problem. GPT and I note that it cancels torque, not net cutting force. The anchor still carries kN-class translation loads.

## Gemini 3.1 Pro


An assessment of T16: Anchoring, hold-down and surface mobility on low-cohesion bodies, evaluated against the revised Phase 0 architecture.

### 1. Evidence
Anchoring in microgravity to react continuous mechanical loads is an unsolved problem. Flight heritage is limited to brief touch-and-go sampling (OSIRIS-REx, 2020; Hayabusa2, 2019), hopping mobility (MINERVA-II, MASCOT, 2018), and failed anchoring attempts (Philae harpoons and ice screws, 2014). Terrestrial laboratory and parabolic flight testing of microspine grippers (JPL Asteroid Redirect Mission studies, Parness et al., ~2013–2017) demonstrated gripping on monolithic basalt and concrete simulants, but not on low-cohesion rubble piles under continuous multi-kilonewton excavation and tether loads.

### 2. Current TRL
**TRL 3–4**. Analytical and experimental proof of concept exists for specific anchoring mechanisms (microspines on monoliths, augers in dense regolith) in 1g and brief microgravity (TRL 3 met). However, component validation in a relevant environment (TRL 5) is unmet, and even laboratory breadboard validation (TRL 4) is highly contested for rubble-pile targets because 1g terrestrial testbeds cannot accurately simulate the low-cohesion, low-gravity granular mechanics of a rubble-pile asteroid under continuous dynamic loading.

### 3. Target and Difficulty
Target is **TRL 6 by KDP-0B**. This is a project-ending technology for Phase 0B; if the mining robots cannot anchor to react the 0.5–5 t/h excavation loads and tether tension, mechanical mining fails. 
**AD² is 7**: Requires fundamental engineering research. The mechanics of reacting high loads against a microgravity rubble pile without locally disrupting the body and causing the anchor to fail are poorly understood, and several competing approaches (augers, microspines, nets, harpoons) exist without a clear path.

### 4. Path
1. **Simulation**: Coupled DEM/FEM modeling of anchor deployment and load-bearing in low-cohesion granular media.
2. **Experiment**: Parabolic flight and drop-tower testing of sub-scale anchoring mechanisms (augers, microspines) in simulated rubble-pile media.
3. **Spaceflight Demonstration**: Phase 0A pathfinder mission to a NEA to deploy and test anchoring mechanisms in true microgravity and regolith conditions.

### 5. Risk and Fallback
**Risk:** project-ending. 
**Fallback:** Abandon mechanical excavation in favor of contactless extraction (e.g., thermal/optical mining) or free-flying containment bags for small boulders, drastically reducing throughput.

### 6. Where others might disagree
Some may argue that microspines are TRL 5 based on JPL's ARM testing, but those tests assumed a monolithic boulder target. The revised architecture must accommodate rubble-pile variants, where microspines are ineffective for reacting high loads.

## GPT-6.1 Sol


## T16 — Anchoring, hold-down and surface mobility on low-cohesion bodies

**Current TRL: 2–3 for the production-scale integrated capability. Target: TRL 6 at KDP-0B. AD²: 7.**

The original entry’s TRL 3 justification is invalid: **model consensus does not demonstrate a critical function.** Physical heritage supports surface interaction, small-scale mobility and anchoring to competent rough surfaces—not sustained reaction of mining loads on a rubble-pile asteroid.

This assessment covers **excavator anchoring, plant and power-tether hold-down, tailings restraint, and relocation/re-anchoring**. It does not rate the bucket-wheel cutter itself.

### Assessment assumptions

- Robots: **2–3.5 t**, excavating **0.5–5 t/h**, at **9–25% duty cycle**.
- Service life: **at least five years**, approximately **3,900–11,000 active excavation hours**, plus continuous exposure and potentially continuous plant/tailings restraint.
- Environment: NEA microgravity, vacuum, thermal cycling at **0.9–1.3 AU**, abrasive and potentially charged regolith, and cumulative radiation.
- Tailings: **13–47 kt/yr**, or **65–235 kt over five years** if retained locally without removal. Tailings containment is a substantial civil/structural function, not merely another robot anchor.
- Excavation loads remain **unverified**. The supplied residual torque range of **0.25–5 kN·m** is a provisional test envelope, not demonstrated performance. At a 1 m effective restraint arm, that corresponds to **0.25–5 kN of differential reaction force**, before adding translational cutting forces, shocks, tether loads or plant loads.
- No absolute target gravity, regolith strength profile, anchor geometry or plant mass is specified. These must be fixed before TRL 5 scaling can be closed.

**Counter-rotation does not eliminate translational excavation forces. Nor does gripping a boulder establish that the boulder itself can react the load without moving.**

## 1. Evidence

| Heritage | Demonstration and environment | Relationship to the requirement |
|---|---|---|
| **Asbeck et al., “Scaling Hard Vertical Surfaces with Compliant Microspine Arrays,” International Journal of Robotics Research, 2006** | Physical terrestrial climbing tests using compliant microspine arrays on rough hard surfaces. Small robot, approximately 0.4 kg; Earth gravity and atmospheric conditions. | Establishes a real anchoring principle for **competent rough surfaces**, not loose regolith. Required robot mass is approximately **5,000–8,750×** the demonstrated robot mass. This is only a size comparison: asteroid anchor sizing must use measured reaction loads, not vehicle weight. No relevant vacuum, rubble-pile stability or five-year demonstration. |
| **Rosetta/Philae, 2014; Biele et al., “The landing(s) of Philae and inferences about comet surface mechanical properties,” Science, 2015** | Approximately 100 kg lander contacted comet 67P in its actual low-gravity space environment. The intended anchoring sequence failed; Philae rebounded and eventually came to rest. | Robot mass ratio **20–35×**. Crucial negative evidence against assuming reliable surface attachment. It does **not** demonstrate successful harpoon/screw hold-down, mining-load reaction or controlled re-anchoring. A comet is also not a validated substitute for the selected NEA surface. |
| **OSIRIS-REx TAG, 2020; Lauretta et al., “Spacecraft sample collection and subsurface excavation of asteroid (101955) Bennu,” Science, 2022** | Approximately 0.3 m sampling head contacted Bennu for roughly six seconds, disturbed the subsurface and collected material. Actual asteroid gravity and space environment. | Demonstrates contact and excavation-related interaction, **not attachment**. Five years is approximately **26 million times** the contact duration. Production anchoring-force and torque ratios are unavailable because TAG did not demonstrate a sustained hold-down capacity. |
| **Hayabusa2/MASCOT, 2018; Jaumann et al., “Images from the surface of asteroid Ryugu show rocks similar to carbonaceous chondrite meteorites,” Science, 2019** | Approximately 9.6 kg lander operated on Ryugu for about 17 hours, including relocation using its internal mobility mechanism. | Required robot mass is approximately **208–365×** larger; five-year duration approximately **2,600×** longer. Demonstrates small, untethered surface relocation—not traction-based travel, hauling, tether management or relocation of a loaded excavator. |

These sources support distinct functions and failure modes. **None demonstrates the required combination of attachment, sustained excavation-load reaction, tethered mobility, tailings restraint and multi-year survival.**

No force-capacity ratio is claimed where the cited demonstration does not establish the relevant capacity.

## 2. Current TRL and unmet exits

### Integrated T16 capability: **TRL 2–3**

- **Lower bound, TRL 2:** documented application concepts exist, and physical heritage establishes feasible principles for selected functions.
- **Upper bound, TRL 3:** defensible only for a narrowly defined critical function—such as engaging rough competent rock—using physical analogue tests. It is **not a demonstrated TRL 3 production anchoring system**.
- **Unmet TRL 4 exit:** no cited integrated breadboard has documented agreement with predictions while reacting representative excavation and tether loads across defined rubble-pile and monolith conditions. The relevant environment and qualification load spectrum are not yet adequately defined.

The uncertainty should remain visible:

| Variant/function | Current assessment | Limitation |
|---|---:|---|
| Competent monolith anchoring: microspines, drilled fixtures or similar | **3–4 for selected components** | Laboratory anchoring heritage exists, but production capacity, asteroid surface variability and life are unproven. |
| Rubble-pile attachment and load transfer | **2–3** | Anchor penetration or boulder gripping does not prove load transfer into a stable body. |
| Tethered production-robot relocation and re-anchoring | **2–3 integrated** | Hopping heritage does not qualify controlled mobility of a tonne-class mining system. |
| Plant and tailings hold-down | **2–3** | No cited asteroid demonstration at the required mass, footprint or lifetime. |

### Metallurgy-route implications

All three routes inherit the same basic T16 gap; none receives additional TRL credit from a design study.

- **No-melt beneficiation/carbonyl or H₂ route:** rated **2–3** for its integrated surface restraint. Process vessels, transfer equipment and tailings still require restraint.
- **Rotating 0.05–0.15 g smelting route:** rated **2–3** for surface restraint. Internal centrifugal acceleration is not automatically transmitted as an equivalent static ground load, but spin-up, imbalance, bearing reactions and faults must be included.
- **Narrow native-metal route with experimentally gated rotating modules:** rated **2–3** until its actual equipment and load interfaces are demonstrated.

The rotating routes add qualification cases; they do not establish an independently higher or lower anchoring TRL without hardware evidence.

## 3. Target, date and difficulty

- **Internal 0A milestones:** TRL **4**, followed by **5**, for selected anchoring and mobility components.
- **KDP-0B:** TRL **6**, without waiver, for the integrated restraint architecture selected for the qualified target class.
- **Needed by:** **KDP-0B, before committing to production deployment.** No calendar date for that gate is supplied.
- **Planning duration:** approximately **7–12 years from a funded start**. If funded in late 2026, that suggests roughly **2033–2038**, not a committed programme date.

**AD²: 7**, using the project’s working anchors.

The difficult step is not manufacturing a stronger anchor. It is establishing a reliable load path through poorly confined, heterogeneous material, then maintaining and verifying that load path while mining changes the terrain. Coupled granular mechanics, autonomy and long-duration restraint require fundamental engineering work.

A target proven to expose extensive competent rock could reduce the difficulty to approximately **AD² 5–6**. That is a target-selection contingency, not evidence that the rubble-pile requirement is solved.

## 4. Development path

Costs below are **rough-order programme allowances in 2026 USD**, not quoted estimates. Tasks overlap; their costs and durations should not simply be summed.

| Step | Scale and method | Cost | Duration | Credible exit |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| **Define loads and audit heritage** | Recover original test data; define six-axis cutting loads, tether transients, plant loads, tailings loads, target gravity and material-property envelopes. Identify where existing tests validate predictions. | $0.5–2M | 0.5–1 yr | No automatic uplift; establish a defensible TRL 3 critical-function case where supported. |
| **Instrumented anchor breadboards** | Full-size anchor elements and representative grain/boulder sizes. Test loose beds, buried competent blocks, fractured rock and monoliths. Include pullout, lateral load, cyclic torque, attachment/release and failure detection. | $3–10M | 1–2 yr | **TRL 4** for tested components. |
| **Validated coupled mechanics** | DEM/structural/control models calibrated against those tests. Model boulder motion, force-chain rearrangement, bed failure, terrain evolution and wheel-load asymmetry. | $2–6M | 1–2 yr | Supports TRL 4–5; simulation alone does not establish TRL 5. |
| **Relevant-environment and life tests** | Production-representative restraint geometry in vacuum and thermal cycling; short reduced-gravity tests plus validated scaling. Include dust, cable loading, wear and radiation-sensitive elements. Qualification addresses 3,900–11,000 active hours and five-year exposure. | $10–30M | 2–4 yr | **TRL 5**, if scaling and life extrapolation are documented and validated. |
| **Integrated restraint and mobility prototype** | Full-load excavator-interface simulator, plant attachment, powered tether and representative tailings enclosure interfaces. Repeated relocation, autonomous proof-loading and fault recovery. Preserve realistic confinement conditions; do not let laboratory walls supply the missing asteroid reaction force. | $15–50M | 2–4 yr | **TRL 5**; a ground rig alone may not resolve relevant low-gravity behaviour. |
| **NEA pathfinder and production-scale qualification closure** | Fly representative anchor/load-path hardware and apply measured excavation-equivalent forces and moments. Demonstrate attachment, sustained cyclic loading, relocation, tether interaction and containment restraint. Complete correlated full-scale and accelerated-life tests. | $150–500M | 4–7 yr | **TRL 6** for the demonstrated, qualified subsystem—not automatically for every target or variant. |

### Essential qualification constraints

1. **A supported regolith tray can give misleadingly good results.** Its walls and floor may supply confinement and reaction forces absent on the asteroid.
2. **Reduced-gravity test duration is a limitation.** Parabolic flight and drop towers inform transient mechanics but cannot establish long-term creep or multi-year attachment.
3. **The 200–600 kg scout is not automatically production-representative.** Required robot mass is **3.3–17.5×** greater. Its pathfinder payload must reproduce the critical anchor geometry, forces, moments and substrate failure domains, or additional demonstration is needed.
4. **Lifetime cannot be asserted from a brief flight success.** Accelerated tests need validated degradation and creep models; otherwise longer exposure or redesign remains necessary.
5. **Both variants need evidence.** A successful monolith demonstration does not qualify rubble-pile operations. KDP-0B may instead explicitly restrict production to the demonstrated target class.

## 5. Risk and fallback

**Risk class: project-ending for the selected 0B production architecture.**

Failure to react excavation loads or restrain tailings prevents safe, reliable production. It does not end 0A research or the wider Dyson programme.

Fallback hierarchy:

1. Select a qualified **competent-rock target** and constrain excavation to demonstrated attachment sites.
2. Change to an **enclosed, internally reacted excavation/processing module**, with its own separately demonstrated capture and structural interfaces.
3. If neither passes the gate, use the pre-committed **“0A only, Earth supply”** outcome.

**Thermal volatile extraction is not an equivalent fallback:** the revised product is Fe-Ni, and thermal extraction does not remove plant, tether or tailings restraint requirements.

## 6. Where others might disagree

- **TRL 3 versus 4:** an assessor focused on a particular terrestrial rock gripper may reasonably assign TRL 4 to that component. Applying it to the full T16 requirement would overextend the evidence.
- **AD² 6 versus 7:** the lower rating is plausible if measured target properties show stable competent rock or a readily enclosed small body. The current rubble-pile requirement does not establish that condition.
- **Whether flight is essential for TRL 6:** NASA TRL 6 does not universally require flight. Here, a convincing ground qualification could suffice only with validated scaling of weak-gravity granular load transfer. I would not assume that scaling is already available.
- **Whether both target variants must pass KDP-0B:** qualifying only the selected target class is defensible if the architecture formally drops the unqualified variant. It is not defensible to claim both variants qualified from one demonstration.

# Consolidated rating: T16 Anchoring, hold-down and surface mobility on low-cohesion bodies

**Panel:** Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-6.1 Sol
**Status:** Two of three models rate 2–3 and one rates 3–4. All three set the target at TRL 6 at KDP-0B, rate AD² 7 and class the risk as project-ending. Timelines diverge by up to a factor of about 2.

## 1. Rating table

| | Claude Opus 5.5 | Gemini 3.1 Pro | GPT-6.1 Sol |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Current TRL** | **2–3** (rubble-pile 2; monolith 2–3; mobility, plant and tailings 2) | **3–4** | **2–3** integrated (monolith components 3–4; rubble-pile, mobility, plant and tailings 2–3) |
| **AD²** | **7** (8 defensible for rubble-pile; monolith alone 5; mobility and tailings 6–7) | **7** | **7** (5–6 if a competent-rock target is confirmed) |
| **Target** | TRL 6 at KDP-0B, no waivers. TRL 4 at 0A mid-term; TRL 5 before pathfinder freeze. | TRL 6 at KDP-0B | TRL 6 at KDP-0B, no waiver. Internal 0A milestones TRL 4–5. |
| **Needed by** | KDP-0B, assumed no earlier than about 2034–2037 | KDP-0B (no date) | KDP-0B before production commitment. About 2033–2038 if funded late 2026. |
| **Risk class** | Project-ending for 0B as currently architected | Project-ending | Project-ending for the 0B production architecture. States it does not end 0A or the wider programme. |
| **Years to target** | **8–14** | **4–8** | **7–12** (from funded start) |
| **Fallback** | Enclosed capture-and-ingest (itself TRL 2); otherwise D-02 "0A only, Earth supply" | Contactless thermal/optical extraction, or free-flying bags for small boulders | Competent-rock target; then enclosed internally reacted module; then "0A only, Earth supply" |
| **Self-stated confidence** | Medium | High | Medium |
| **Record ID used** | `asteroid-anchoring-holddown-mobility` (new, split from parent) | `t16-anchoring-mobility` | `asteroid-mining-bucket-wheel` (parent ID retained) |

## 2. Where the models agree

- **The March 2026 TRL 3 basis is invalid.** Claude and GPT both state that "multi-model consensus" is not evidence. Gemini does not discuss the prior entry but reaches its rating on separate grounds.
- **No heritage demonstrates sustained anchoring under load on a small body.** All three cite:
  - Philae as a failed anchoring attempt;
  - OSIRIS-REx TAG as brief contact without hold-down;
  - Hayabusa2 hopping landers as small, unanchored mobility.
- **Target is TRL 6 at KDP-0B.** No model proposes a waiver.
- **AD² is 7 for the rubble-pile requirement as stated.** Claude and GPT both say a competent-rock target would lower it, to 5 and 5–6 respectively.
- **Risk class is project-ending** at the 0B level.
- **An NEA pathfinder demonstration is on the critical path to TRL 6.** All three paths end with it. GPT adds that flight is not universally required for TRL 6, but says it would not assume the needed ground scaling is available.
- **Counter-rotation cancels torque, not net translational cutting force** (Claude and GPT). Gemini's submission does not address this point.
- **The two target variants need separate evidence** (Claude and GPT). A monolith demonstration does not qualify rubble-pile operation. Both say KDP-0B could instead formally restrict production to the demonstrated target class.
- **Scale ratios are mutually consistent where they overlap.** For example, Claude gives OSIRIS-REx contact duration as about 3 × 10⁷× short and GPT gives about 2.6 × 10⁷×.

## 3. Where the models diverge, and why

### 3.1 Current TRL: 2–3 (Claude, GPT) vs 3–4 (Gemini)

**Gemini's basis.** It treats TRL 3 as met by two things:
- microspines on monoliths, in 1 g and parabolic flight, citing JPL ARM / Parness et al., about 2013–2017;
- "augers in dense regolith." No source is given for the auger claim.

Gemini's upper bound of 4 rests on component breadboards. However, Gemini also calls TRL 4 "highly contested for rubble-pile targets," and states its unmet exit criterion at TRL 5. That implies TRL 4 is met. Its rating text and its exit criterion are not fully consistent.

**Claude's basis.**
- TRL 3 is unmet for rubble-pile, mobility and tailings. No pull-out, cyclic-load or retention test has been run against a prior prediction in Pa-cohesion or cohesion-scaled media.
- TRL 4 is unmet even for monolith. Two items are missing: a documented relevant-environment definition (boulder strength is only thermally inferred), and a kN-class, 10⁶-cycle breadboard test.
- Claude treats OSIRIS-REx, Hayabusa2 SCI and low-g penetration data as validating regolith properties, not anchor function.

**GPT's basis.**
- It largely aligns with Gemini on scope for monolith components, rating them 3–4.
- It rates the integrated capability 2–3, because "anchor penetration or boulder gripping does not prove load transfer into a stable body."

**Partly a scope difference.** Gemini's 3–4 is close to GPT's component-level rating for monolith anchoring. The disagreement is sharpest on whether component evidence on competent rock can set the composite rating. Claude says the weaker variant governs while the D-02 target gate is open.

**What would settle it:**
- Retrieval of the original JPL microspine test records: load values, parabolic-flight results, and whether predictions were documented beforehand. Claude marks the Parness load values and any zero-g tests as unsure. Gemini marks its microspine claim as confident but gives no specific paper or test report.
- A source for the "augers in dense regolith" claim.
- A pull-out or cyclic test against prediction in cohesion-scaled granular media. This is Step 2 of the consolidated path below.

### 3.2 Years to target: 4–8 (Gemini) vs 7–12 (GPT) vs 8–14 (Claude)

| Driver | Gemini | GPT | Claude |
|---|---|---|---|
| Path length | 3 steps; jumps from TRL 4 straight to the TRL 6 flight demo, with no explicit TRL 5 step | 6 steps; explicit TRL 5 relevant-environment and life qualification | 7 steps; adds scout geotechnical payload and tailings and mobility breadboards |
| Long-duration evidence | Not addressed | Accelerated life tests with validated creep and degradation models | At least 6–12 months in situ plus a 5-yr-equivalent ground life test |
| Scout in-situ characterisation | Not included | Not a separate step | 20–60 M per scout over 4–7 yr including cruise |
| Pathfinder cost | 50–150 M | 150–500 M | 150–500 M |

Claude also raises an open governance question. If "no waivers" is read as requiring 5 years in situ, KDP-0B slips by about 5 years. Neither other model addresses this reading.

**What would settle it:**
- A board ruling on whether TRL 6 requires multi-year in-situ exposure.
- A ruling on whether a TRL 5 relevant-environment step can be skipped.
- A stated KDP-0B date.

### 3.3 Fallback

- **Gemini** proposes contactless thermal/optical extraction.
- **Claude and GPT** both reject thermal extraction as an equivalent fallback. Their reasons: the revised product is native Fe-Ni, and thermal extraction still requires plant, tether and tailings restraint.
- **Shared ground:** Gemini's boulder-bagging option overlaps with Claude's enclosed capture-and-ingest and with GPT's internally reacted enclosed module. Claude rates that option itself at TRL 2.
- **GPT only** proposes restricting production to a qualified competent-rock target as the first fallback.

**What would settle it:** confirmation of the product definition (Fe-Ni) and of whether any contactless route avoids surface restraint. No model presents evidence that one does.

### 3.4 Microspines and boulder grip on rubble piles

- **Gemini** asserts microspines are "ineffective for reacting high loads" on rubble piles.
- **Claude** lists boulder grip as one of three candidate rubble-pile load paths, untested.
- **GPT** says gripping a boulder does not establish that the boulder can react the load without moving.

None cites a test.

**What would settle it:** a boulder-grip pull-out test in a cohesion-scaled matrix that measures boulder displacement, together with in-situ boulder-interlock data from scouts.

### 3.5 Load envelope definition

- **Claude** assumes a peak net cutting force of 0.5–20 kN, derived as P/v_tip. It also gives a single-wheel torque case of 2.5–95 kN·m and assumes a plant mass of 50–500 t.
- **GPT** converts the 0.25–5 kN·m residual torque to 0.25–5 kN at a 1 m arm. It calls all loads unverified and plant mass unspecified.
- **Gemini** states the requirement as reacting "0.5–5 t/h excavation loads." That is a throughput figure, not a force; the other two express loads in kN and kN·m.

**What would settle it:** the rq-0-26 DEM six-axis force and torque spectra. Claude's Step 1 and GPT's Step 1 both call for these.

### 3.6 Rotating-smelter load interface

- **Claude** says the rotating route adds spin-reaction loads to the plant mount, and that castable slag could ease tailings retention.
- **GPT** says internal centrifugal acceleration is not automatically transmitted as an equivalent static ground load, but spin-up, imbalance, bearing and fault loads must be included.
- **Gemini** does not address route interfaces.

These positions differ in emphasis rather than conclusion. Both Claude and GPT require the rotating-route load cases in qualification.

### 3.7 Counter-rotation attribution

Claude states that "Gemini treats [counter-rotation] as solving the reaction problem." That position does not appear in Gemini's T16 submission. It may refer to the rq-0-26 deliberation, which is not part of this record. The attribution is noted but cannot be verified here.

### 3.8 Record scope and ID

The three models use three different IDs:
- Claude explicitly splits T16 off `asteroid-mining-bucket-wheel`;
- GPT keeps the parent ID while stating it does not rate the cutter;
- Gemini uses a new ID.

The board needs to fix the record identity before the rating is entered.

### 3.9 Internal inconsistencies flagged for authors

- **Gemini:**
  - Rates TRL 3–4, but calls TRL 4 contested and states its unmet exit criterion at TRL 5.
  - Its path credits TRL 3 from simulation alone.
  - Its path goes from TRL 4 to TRL 6 with no TRL 5 step.
- **GPT:**
  - Step 1 (literature and heritage audit) is coded `reaches_trl: 3` in the YAML, while the prose says "No automatic uplift."
  - Its unmet-exit text says "a conservative TRL 2 assessment also requires validated critical-function evidence." Validated critical-function evidence is a TRL 3 criterion elsewhere in the same submission.
- **Claude:** none identified.

## 4. Evidence base

### 4.1 Cited by all three models

| Evidence | What it shows | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Rosetta/Philae, 2014; Biele et al., *Science* 2015 | Intended anchoring failed and the lander rebounded. Negative evidence. | Strongest shared item. Claude and GPT both cite the paper; Gemini cites the mission. |
| OSIRIS-REx TAG, 2020; Lauretta et al., *Science* 2022 | About 6 s of contact; low resistance; no hold-down | Claude marks the exact resistance values as unsure. Gemini gives no paper. |
| Hayabusa2 MASCOT (and MINERVA-II, per Claude and Gemini), 2018 | kg-class unanchored hopping and relocation | GPT alone cites Jaumann et al., *Science* 2019 (9.6 kg, about 17 h). Claude marks MINERVA-II operational duration as unsure. |

### 4.2 Microspines: confidence conflict

| Model | Source cited | Scale given | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude | Parness et al., *Journal of Field Robotics* 2013 | About 10² N per gripper | Paper: yes. Load values and zero-g tests: **unsure**. |
| Gemini | "JPL ARM studies (Parness et al., ~2013–2017)," including parabolic flight | 10–100 N | **Confident**, but no specific paper or test report is given |
| GPT | Asbeck et al., *International Journal of Robotics Research* 2006 (**GPT only**) | About 0.4 kg robot, 1 g, terrestrial | Confident |

This is the evidence item on which Gemini's higher TRL most depends. It is also the one where the models disagree on confidence.

### 4.3 Single-model citations

**Claude only, marked confident:**
- Spohn et al. 2015 (MUPUS);
- InSight HP³ mole failure;
- Walsh et al. 2022;
- Arakawa et al. 2020 (Hayabusa2 SCI; exact cohesion bound unsure);
- Lauretta et al. 2019 (Bennu particle ejection);
- Hayabusa MINERVA loss, 2005;
- NEAR Shoemaker on Eros;
- Scheeres et al. 2010 (cohesion scaling);
- Sánchez & Scheeres 2014 ("mostly").

**Claude only, marked unsure:**
- Grott et al. 2019 (exact values unsure);
- Rozitis et al. 2020;
- DART follow-up cohesion papers;
- Colwell COLLIDE/PRIME and Murdoch drop-tower work (specifics unsure);
- STRATA-1 (results unsure);
- ARM ground tests (explicitly not counted).

**GPT only:** Asbeck et al. 2006; Jaumann et al. 2019.
